title: Is it just my impression or is 3D much easier to create with AI than 2D?
author: Kind-Being-5369
selftext:
You can find a bunch of videos on YT about how to create 3D assets for games.  
Some videos show production ready models (as long as you aren't creating some AAA perfect looking game).  
Meanwhile, if you search for 2D assets you can only find stupid looking art which can't be used for real products.  
If we are talking about 2D pixel art, then it's even worse.  
It seems to me that generative AI for 3D is advancing MUCH FASTER than for 2D.  
I know that 3D games are generally harder to make, but if you take in consideration that you can get better results in 3D, then it may not make that much difference in the end.  
  
Anyone else feeling the same?  
  
I've always loved pixel art games, but I'm not an artist (I already tried and I just to enjoy the process of drawing).  
I'm considering trying to make a 3D game just because it's easier to generate original assets.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
Tripo does. Tripo can get you down to 2-5k polys which, while not  fantastic, is acceptable for games expecting a AAA system requirement. I don't know if Meshy has caught up to them or not.

I disagree on this with pineappleoptics. Generally if you're looking for truly stylized low poly experience, then they're right that the models aren't there. But for a high fidelity PBR game, you're expecting the poly counts they push out and should be able to handle it fine in something like Unreal Engine. But try pulling those same models into Godot and your game is going to run 10x worse than it would if you were just sculpting an equivalent low poly by hand in Blender.

Whether or not it can work for you depends heavily on your game and what it actually is.

replies.author: ScrumptiousChildren
replies.body:
It’s like patchwork. It’s fine for a single artifact of clothing or some map assets, if you’re willing to put up with the questionable texturing or topology. 

But if you want to generate a full character, for example, the rigging and animation would be messy, some vertices weird, artifacts like that. The amount of time you have to spend fixing things is hardly worth the time. 

Perhaps with a strong pipeline and certain caveats you could speed up your workflow but it’s not a clear cut win.

comments.author: Plastic_Pause_8329
comments.body:
Prompt and giving your agent access to the right tools i think makes all the difference. 

Prompt: try giving it examples of amazing looking 2d games to compare against literally give it screenshots and say compare these side by side to match quality. 

For 2d it will need quality image generation tools, i use flux locally, or if you have access to openai, let it been images through that. 

Describe well what you want in your game e.g. stunning backgrounds (describe them and include, examples of quality to match), describe foreground, e.g. is everything destructive? Fall apart? 

It does have strengths, learn them by looking at other games and lean on its strengths as that will make it better. 

The same concept works to make a better looking 3d game.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
Low poly models... like actual true low poly models, are in the hundreds of faces. An industry equivalent low poly character from something like Synty would be a few hundred polys. A detailed crate would be \~100 faces. Etc.

If you generate those same things with the industry leader in smart topo (at least i believe Tripo still is) you can push it down to 2-5k polys and still have something that isn't completely warped and broken. If this only happened with characters it wouldn't be a huge deal. But no, a standard crate or refrigerator is going to be 2-5k, meaning 20-50x the size. That's fine in a game that's not meant to be low poly, like a AAA PBR release. Those games expect millions of polys on the screen at once because UE has tech that allows it without any issue. But in some kind of Godot low poly game that's publishing to web and/or mobile, you generally have a budget of 300-500k polys on the screen at any given time. This can be quickly eclipsed depending on FOV, object density, etc. And all these budgets are not factoring in things like shaders or dynamic lighting which multiply in demands depending on polys on the screen.

So really that's the big difference between hand-making your objects vs using AI. There's still a large multiplier in performance drain. Again, not an issue if you're not true low poly, and if I was working in UE I'd probably be using 3d genned assets. But until UE actually gets powerful AI tools for blueprint integration I don't intend to try my hand at it.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
1. Yes, to some extent. You can get fairly reasonable 3d models, just as you can get fairly reasonable 2d sprites from AI. But both require manual work and processing at their base, and this gets further increased depending on what you're trying to do with them. Generating a crate is far different from generating a model that needs  animations, or different skins/equipment. Additionally, 3d has virtually zero support for animations that aren't humanoid (and the animations are pretty bad imo, but I have always preferred stylized games, so that may be a 'Me' thing.)  
2. Whatever you're looking at for your 2d art comparison though is completely off-base. You can generate anything imaginable in 2d if you know what you're doing. Most people don't \[know what they're doing\] though. The hard part is making sure you have consistency in styles, not in individual quality. For pixel art you need to process it to actually be pixel art, which is its own minor process. However an advantage to pixel art is that you don't need to be a traditional artist to make it. It helps tremendously understanding color theory, light/shadows, etc, but you don't need a hand that's practiced in clean strokes, and the audience won't hold it against you when your character is a 16x16 sprite, meaning you don't need strict anatomical detail. Rather you just need an understanding of what 'looks' good especially in a retro sense. Anyone can make pixel art. Not necessarily well, but anyone can make it, and when you're working with a base that you've generated with AI and the burden is simply on you to refine and polish (and most importantly animate since pixel animations by AI are not generally true pixel animations) you can jump into it even faster.

But yes, 3d will likely continue to outpace 2d in terms of AI support. This is the avenue companies are focusing on because it appeals most to AAA studios as well as outside the game industry, for Hollywood, architecture, etc. If you're making an action game, there aren't a lot of good reasons to go 2d pixel if you're using AI imo, at least not in terms of fidelity vs workload, unless you're just trying to make a highly accessible game that even potatoes can run.

comments.author: imnotabot303
comments.body:
The guy in the video is trying to sell courses, on top of that he's being sponsored by an AI 3D platform. The whole video is essentially an ad.

3D isn't easier than 2D, both require a lot of manual work unless you're happy with aI looking low quality assets.

You might get lucky with the occasional asset coming out ok but it depends on what you're making and even then it's going to need a lot of cleanup and optimisation. 3D generally involves a lot more disciplines and technical skills than 2D art. 

I think the issue is that a lot of people using AI lack 3D knowledge so are unaware of all the small problems and issues that come with making game ready models. They just want something they can generate, auto rig, slap on some Miximo animations and call it a day. In that respect it can seem easier but that's just because you would be making low quality assets.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
Yeah it's a bit of a weird situation because currently you need to be experienced with 3D to make good use of generated 3D assets, however most people experienced with 3D are not going to use them because all it's really doing is removing the fun part, as in the actual modelling and texturing. So what you're left with is AI doing the fun part and you just left doing a bunch of monkey work with all the technical cleanup and prep. 

I think it's going to be like this for a while imo. 3D art is a lot different to 2D because it's more technical. Artists are constantly making technical decisions during the process which AI isn't. The AI is essentially just trying to spit out a model within the specified poly count and texture size.

Think of current generative 3D more like 3D scanning or photogrammetry, it's just one step in a much bigger workflow. 

2D is a much easier route to take if you're making your first game and have no experience with 3D asset creation.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
Myself I'm fairly competent at 3D as I've been doing it for over 20 years so unless I had a lot of assets to create it doesn't really offer much of an advantage for me right now. I'm sure that's true of most competent 3D artists.

The last time I experimented with it, I found the best option is to treat it like any other scan or photogrammetry asset. So instead of using the asset itself you use it as a template.

You either do this by just using it as a 3D reference model to build your own around it or if the model is fairly accurate you can do a retopology workflow which is essentially creating a new clean mesh on the surface of the generated model. This gives you the ability to create a much lower poly mesh and also be in control of your edge flow for potential animation deformation of the mesh or just reducing the chance of surface rendering artifacts.

After that you can UV unwrap your new mesh and then bake the generated textures from the AI mesh to your new mesh.

Textures is a whole new issue too as from what I've seen generated models often don't have the best textures so you will likely also need to make manual fixes.

Personally I think we are potentially still 5 years or so out from 3D gen being good enough useful in the game industry. Even then I doubt it's going to be perfect and will require manual work.

It's definitely got it's uses right now for pre rendered work though, like quick and easy background assets.
